written_by: SENTINEL editors, revised from the earlier dashboard essay; facts checked by web search on 16 October 2026
lede: Organized crime is not a separate crime beat in Latin America. It is a force inside civil–military relations: illicit economies decide where armies deploy, which police forces can be trusted, and who bargains with whom over territory and prisons.

sections.title: Cocaine at record levels, and the rents that come with it
paras: Cocaine remains the hemisphere's dominant illicit commodity. Colombia's coca crop reached about 261,000 hectares in 2024, up from 253,000 a year earlier, and its potential cocaine output in 2023 was 2,664 tonnes, 53% more than in 2022.
Worldwide production reached a record of roughly 4,100 tonnes in 2024.
Trafficking routes through Central America, the Caribbean and the Pacific drive military deployments, corruption and cartel–state conflict across most of the countries SENTINEL monitors.

Fentanyl reaching the United States is made mostly in Mexico, by the Sinaloa and Jalisco cartels, from precursor chemicals imported largely from Asia. It has become the main driver of US terrorist designations and of friction between Washington and Mexico City.
Illegal gold mining funds armed groups in Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, Peru and Brazil, and draws military units into protection and territorial control.

sections.title: Transnational gangs and the terrorist designations
paras: In February 2025 the United States designated eight Latin American criminal groups as foreign terrorist organizations, among them the Sinaloa and Jalisco cartels, Tren de Aragua and MS-13. Haiti's Viv Ansanm and Gran Grif followed in May, Ecuador's Los Lobos and Los Choneros and the Barrio 18 gang in September, Venezuela's Cartel de los Soles in November and Colombia's Clan del Golfo in December 2025.
The list kept growing in 2026, with Brazil's two largest gangs, the PCC and Comando Vermelho, two more Mexican cartels and two more Ecuadorian gangs, and stood at 21 in September 2026.

The designations turned counternarcotics into a counterterrorism mission, and they are the legal frame the Pentagon has used for its strikes on boats in the Caribbean and the eastern Pacific since September 2025.

sections.title: State capture and the corruption of security forces
paras: Criminal penetration of the security forces is the longest-term threat organized crime poses to civilian control. In Honduras, former president Juan Orlando Hernández, convicted in New York in 2024 of drug trafficking that ran through the state's security apparatus and sentenced to 45 years, was pardoned by President Trump in December 2025.

In Venezuela, Washington designated the Cartel de los Soles, which it describes as headed by Nicolás Maduro and senior officers, a terrorist organization in November 2025, weeks before US forces captured Maduro in Caracas.
In Haiti, the Viv Ansanm gang federation was estimated in June 2026 to control about 70% of Port-au-Prince.

In Mexico, the army has taken over policing, intelligence and customs without ending collusion at state and municipal level. These cases are not aberrations. They are the predictable result of sending armed forces into high-rent illicit economies without civilian oversight.

frontlines.text: Cartel fragmentation, military policing and the heaviest sustained collision between organized crime and state force.
The clearest case of criminal violence turned into an 'internal armed conflict' and an expanded military role; voters rejected foreign bases in November 2025.
Gang control of the capital, a hollowed state, and a UN-authorized Gang Suppression Force still far below strength.
Criminal governance, cross-border networks and the political uses of irregular armed actors after Maduro's capture.
Record coca, armed groups contesting territory, and a new government that has replaced negotiation with offensive operations.
